svg.title: 2. Scenario: pod IP exhaustion and the fix
svg.text: Before: default VPC CNI, pods share the node subnets
3 node subnets x /20 = 12,273 usable IPs, shared by nodes and pods
kubelet: FailedCreatePodSandBox ... failed to assign an IP address to container
After: pods get their own non-routable range, in /28 prefixes
ENI 2, ENI 3: attached only when needed
up to 14 prefixes x 16 IPs each
3 pod subnets x /18 = 49,137 usable pod IPs (100.64.0.0/16 is a VPC secondary CIDR)
How traffic flows once pods live in 100.64.0.0/16
Scenario: the load test that ran the VPC out of IPs, and the networking that fixed it (VPC CNI custom networking + /28 prefixes)
Load test, Thursday 19:40. HPA asks for 9,600 pods. At ~205 nodes and ~6,400 pods:
Pods sit in ContainerCreating, new nodes cannot even get a primary IP, checkout p99
climbs from 180 ms to 2.4 s, and the test is stopped at 67% of the target.
Quick relief that night: MINIMUM_IP_TARGET=30 and WARM_IP_TARGET=4 on the aws-node DaemonSet
(~36 IPs per node instead of ~60, at the cost of more EC2 API calls).
48 IPs for 32 pods, and one EC2 call
300 nodes x 48 IPs = ~14,400 needed vs 49,137 available
Retest two weeks later: 9,600 pods on 296 nodes, zero IP errors, pod
scheduled-to-running p95 down from 21 s to 9 s (fewer EC2 calls per pod).
Rolled out by creating new Karpenter NodePools that point at an EC2NodeClass
with the new settings, then draining the old pools with a 10% disruption budget.
No node ever mixed secondary IPs and prefixes.
Long-term option for new clusters: IPv6 (chosen at cluster creation, cannot be changed).
1. Inbound: the ALB lives in routable subnets and sends straight to pod IPs inside the VPC.
2. Outbound beyond the VPC: the CNI rewrites the source to the node IP, so 100.64.0.0/16 never needs a route anywhere else.
3. Service-to-service across VPCs and accounts: VPC Lattice, which also handles overlapping CIDRs.
Security groups for pods and network policies still apply to pod IPs in the 100.64 range.
